title: S3 Performance & Low-Latency Access
summary: Request rates, multipart upload, Transfer Acceleration, byte-range fetches and S3 Express One Zone.
tldr: S3 scales **per prefix**: spread hot keys across more prefixes to get more requests per second.
Big or unreliable uploads → **multipart upload** (parallel, retry only failed parts). Far-away users → **Transfer Acceleration** through CloudFront edge locations.
Big downloads → parallel **byte-range GETs**. Millions of small requests with single-digit-ms latency in one AZ → **S3 Express One Zone** directory buckets.
An app that needs a file path over S3 data, read-heavy and writing new files only → **Mountpoint for Amazon S3**.

keyFacts.text: Requests per second **per prefix**: 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD. HTTP 503 Slow Down means spread keys across more prefixes.
Consider multipart above about 100 MB; a single PUT can't exceed 5 GB. Up to 10,000 parts per upload.
Maximum S3 object size since December 2025 (it was 5 TB). Objects that large must use multipart upload.
**S3 Express One Zone** stores data in one AZ in a *directory bucket*, with much lower latency and lower request cost than S3 Standard.
S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs and DELETEs. No extra wait or setting is needed.

traps: Transfer Acceleration helps long internet paths, not in-Region EC2 reads or request-rate limits.
Versioning doesn't increase throughput; it only keeps old versions.
S3 Express One Zone lives in one AZ, so use it for data you can regenerate or that has another copy.
Mountpoint isn't a full POSIX file system. It doesn't support editing existing files in place, so don't pick it for shared read-write workloads (use EFS or FSx).
A gateway VPC endpoint gives private routing and avoids NAT cost; it doesn't add bandwidth.
Glacier storage classes can't be mounted or read directly at low latency.
